# Modal System Design of Multirobot Systems by Interaction Mode Control

Seiichiro Katsura, Member, IEEE, and Kiyoshi Ohishi, Member, IEEE

**Abstract—Motion control technology in an open environment will be more important. Future motion systems should interact with other systems or environments. To adapt to complicated environments and do tasks, a realization of multi-degree-of-freedom motion is necessary for human cooperating motion. This paper proposes a unified control approach for multirobot systems by interaction mode control. The proposed interaction mode control considers only interactions between systems. The interactions are abstracted by using mode quarry matrices. Since the transformed modes are independent of each other, it is possible to design a controller in decoupled modal space. This paper also proposes a novel control index named “hybrid ratio.” Hybrid ratio is defined as the influence of external acceleration input on the acceleration response of a system. Since it is possible to realize the assigned hybrid ratio in each mode according to the task, the motion command with hybrid ratio is represented as task code. Thus, the interaction mode control is able to be treated as task kinematics. The proposed interaction mode control is applied for grasping motion by multirobot systems. The numerical and experimental results show the viability of the proposed method.**

**Index Terms—Acceleration control, disturbance observer, haptics, hybrid control, interaction mode control, modal decomposition, motion control, multirobot systems.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

M <sup>OTION</sup> control technology [1], [2] has been widely usedin industry applications. Software servoing technology is now common in machine tools, robotics, and mechatronics. It has been intensively developed for numerical control machines and disturbance rejection. Since ideal position control has infinite gain against position error, it has infinite stiffness. Position control is effective and robust for relatively simple tasks with low-degree-of-freedom (DOF) applications, such as an X–Y table of machine tool and joint control of industrial robot. Such applications exist in a closed space, and motion area is limited in a small space.

However, a robot will be expected to play the role of a human’s partner in an aging society with fewer children [3], [4]. Human-friendly robots are beginning to spread in society. Pet robots, welfare robots, and home robots can be considered as human-friendly robots. Such robots will move in open space rather than in limited space. They will contact various environments and do their tasks. Recently developed robots are required to have the ability to contact with an unknown environment. Conventional motion control will not always be suitable for future applications due to its lack of adaptive capability with the environment. A more sophisticated ability in motion control is necessary for compliant contact with the environment.

Acceleration control is the best solution for compliant motion to an unknown environment [5]–[7]. Acceleration control makes a motion system a zero-stiffness system without losing robustness. Thus, it is possible to set various control stiffnesses corresponding to task motions.

Acceleration control is essential also for the integration of multi-DOF motion. Usually, a motion controller of a multi-DOF manipulator is designed with respect to the Cartesian coordinate system. Control stiffness is assigned in each work space according to task motions. The relationship between the work space and joint space is very important for the control of a multi-DOF manipulator. To integrate the various control stiffnesses in the joint space, each motion reference with respect to the work space should be transformed into an acceleration reference.

Motion control technology in an open environment will be more important [8]. Future motion systems should interact with other systems or environments. To adapt to complicated environments and do tasks, the realization of multi-DOF motion is necessary for human-cooperating motion. Cooperation control architectures of multirobot systems have been proposed in order to realize complicated tasks, such as grasping operation [9]–[12], formation control of mobile robots [13]–[16], and bilateral teleoperation [17]–[20]. Conventional coordinate transformation with respect to the Cartesian coordinate system is not always suitable for cooperation control of dexterous tasks including grasping motion. In controlling multirobot systems, it is important to consider the interactions between systems.

This paper proposes a unified-control approach for multirobot systems by interaction mode control. The proposed interaction mode control considers only the interactions between systems. The interactions are abstracted by using mode quarry matrices [21]–[23]. The mode quarry matrices transform each physical parameter of systems into modal parameters. Since the transformed modes are independent of each other, it is possible to design a controller in decoupled modal space. The acceleration references in each mode are integrated and realized in each joint system through the inverse modal transformation. Thus, the mode quarry matrices are regarded as the spatial filter between its mechanisms and task motions.

This paper also proposes a novel control index named “hybrid ratio.” Hybrid ratio is defined as the influence of external acceleration input on the acceleration response of the system. Since it is possible to realize the assigned hybrid ratio in each mode according to task motions, motion command with the hybrid ratio is represented as task code. Thus, the interaction mode control is able to be treated as modal kinematics. As a result, an intuitive control design is attained by the proposed method.

This paper is organized as follows. Section II shows the importance of acceleration control in motion control. In Section III, the interaction mode control is proposed. The proposed interaction mode control is applied to grasping motion in Section IV. In Section V, this paper is summarized.

## II. ACCELERATION CONTROL IN MOTION CONTROL

## A. Target of Motion Control

A motion controller in an open environment will require various stiffnesses corresponding to each task. Control stiffness [2] is defined in the following equation:

$$
\kappa = \frac {\partial f}{\partial x}\tag{1}
$$

where $\kappa$ denotes control stiffness, f denotes generated force, and x denotes position. The ideal position control should have infinite stiffness; however, the ideal force control should have zero stiffness. A modern motion system requires the ability to be compliant with a contact environment. Motion control should take plural modes of environment into account. The environmental information is a key to be compliant to an unknown environment. Motion control taking environmental information into account will make various machines including robots more adaptive and versatile.

## B. Robustness in Motion Systems

Recent dexterous motion requires a wide range of control stiffness. For example, an electronic-parts-inserting machine needs some compliant motion at the tip of the machine. This case requires low or no control stiffness. The conventional controller will have very low forward gain for such a purpose and will lose robustness as a result. To satisfy such varied requirements, the controller should have variable control stiffness, keeping the system highly robust.

Acceleration control can set the control stiffness independent of robustness. A disturbance observer [2], [24] is a good candidate for attaining robust acceleration control. A disturbance observer identifies the total mechanical load torque and parameter change. In other words, the identification of disturbance torque is essential for motion control robustness to realize various applications.

## C. Integration of Multi-DOF Motion

Acceleration control is essential also for the integration of multi-DOF motion. Usually, the relationship between the work space and the joint space is very important for the control of a multi-DOF manipulator. For instance, the velocity relationship of a three-DOF manipulator is defined as follows:

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c} \dot {x} \\ \dot {y} \\ \dot {z} \end{array} \right] = \boldsymbol {J} _ {\mathrm{aco}} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \dot {\theta} _ {1} \\ \dot {\theta} _ {2} \\ \dot {\theta} _ {3} \end{array} \right]\tag{2}
$$

$$
\dot {X} = J _ {\mathrm{aco}} \dot {\theta}\tag{3}
$$

where $\boldsymbol { J } _ { \mathrm { a c o } }$ denotes the Jacobian matrix. $\dot { x }$ and $\dot { \theta }$ denote the velocity response with respect to the work space and the joint space, respectively.

As the hybrid position/force control [25]–[28] is installed to the three-DOF manipulator, the motion with respect to the Z-axis is constrained by the environment, and the other motion with respect to the $\dot { X { - } Y }$ plane is controlled by position servoing. Hence, the control stiffness with respect to the Z-axis should be $0 ,$ and the control stiffness with respect to the $X { - } Y$ plane should be $\infty .$ It is difficult for a conventional motion controller to realize the various control stiffnesses in each joint. To integrate the various control stiffnesses in the joint space, each motion reference with respect to the work space should be transformed into the following acceleration reference:

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c} \ddot {\theta} _ {1} \\ \dot {\theta} _ {2} \\ \ddot {\theta} _ {3} \end{array} \right] \approx J _ {\mathrm{aco}} ^ {- 1} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \ddot {x} \\ \ddot {y} \\ \ddot {z} \end{array} \right]\tag{4}
$$

$$
\ddot {\theta} \approx J _ {\mathrm{aco}} ^ {- 1} \ddot {X}\tag{5}
$$

where $\ddot { x }$ and $\ddot { \theta }$ denote the acceleration response with respect to the work space and the joint space, respectively. Since the effect of the derivation of Jacobian is little, (5) is able to be regarded as the inverse matrix of the derivation of (3).

## D. Acceleration Control by Disturbance Observer

This subsection introduces an acceleration control by using a disturbance observer. A disturbance observer is designed to cancel the disturbance torque as quickly as possible. The estimated disturbance torque is obtained from the velocity response $\hat { \dot { \theta } } _ { m }$ and the current reference $I ^ { \mathrm { r e f } }$ , as shown in Fig. 1. The velocity response is calculated by the derivative of position response, which is detected by a position encoder. $g _ { \mathrm { p d } }$ denotes the cutoff frequency of the pseudo-derivation.

The disturbance torque $\tau ^ { \mathrm { d i s } }$ is represented as

$$
\tau^ {\mathrm{dis}} = (J _ {m} - J _ {m n}) \ddot {\theta} _ {m} + (K _ {t n} - K _ {t}) I ^ {\mathrm{ref}} + F _ {c} + D \dot {\theta} _ {m} + \tau^ {\mathrm{ext}}\tag{6}
$$

where

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \text {node} & \\ J _ {m} & \text {motor inertia;} \\ K _ {t} & \text {torque constant;} \\ F _ {c} & \text {Coulomb friction;} \\ D \dot {\theta} _ {m} & \text {viscous friction;} \\ \tau^ {\mathrm{ext}} & \text {external torque;} \\ \text {subscript n} & \text {nominal value.} \end{array}
$$

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 1. Block diagram of the disturbance observer.

In (6), the first term is the torque due to the self-inertia variation. The second term is torque pulsations due to the variation of the torque coefficient.

The following equation shows that the disturbance torque is estimated through a first-order low-pass filter:

$$
\hat {\tau} ^ {\mathrm{dis}} = \frac {\frac {J _ {m n}}{J _ {m}} g _ {\mathrm{dis}}}{s + \frac {K _ {t}}{K _ {t n}} \frac {J _ {m n}}{J _ {m}} g _ {\mathrm{dis}}} \tau^ {\mathrm{dis}}\tag{7}
$$

where $g _ { \mathrm { d i s } }$ denotes the cutoff frequency of the low-pass filter. The disturbance torque estimated by (7) is used for a realization of robust motion control. The compensation current for the disturbance torque $I ^ { \mathrm { c m p } }$ is calculated as follows:

$$
I ^ {\mathrm{cmp}} = \frac {1}{K _ {t n}} \hat {\tau} ^ {\mathrm{dis}}.\tag{8}
$$

The robust motion controller makes a motion system an acceleration control system, as shown in Fig. 2. As shown in Fig. 2, the effect of the disturbance torque is represented as a transfer function $G _ { s }$ , which is defined as

$$
G _ {s} = \frac {s}{s + g _ {\mathrm{dis}} ^ {*}}\tag{9}
$$

$$
g _ {\mathrm{dis}} ^ {*} = \frac {K _ {t}}{K _ {t n}} \frac {J _ {m n}}{J _ {m}} g _ {\mathrm{dis}}.\tag{10}
$$

$G _ { s }$ represents a sensitivity showing how the disturbance torque influences the motion system and is called a sensitivity function. As a result, the acceleration reference $\ddot { \theta } _ { m } ^ { \mathrm { r e f } }$ is attainable within the bandwidth of the disturbance observer.

## III. INTERACTION MODE CONTROL

This paper proposes a unified control approach for multirobot systems by interaction mode control. The proposed interaction mode control considers only the interactions between systems. The interaction mode is obtained by using mode quarry matrices. The hybrid ratio is proposed as the control index of the modal control design. Each modal control is easily integrated, since all transmitted information is based on acceleration.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 2. Acceleration control system by the disturbance observer.

## A. Hybrid Ratio

As the control system is based on acceleration control, the system is represented as Fig. 3. The input of the system is the acceleration reference of the controller and the equivalent acceleration from other systems by force feedback $\ddot { \theta } ^ { \mathrm { e x t } }$ . The disturbance torque is compensated, and only the external torque is fed back by using the disturbance observer. A stiff-position servo controller should realize the acceleration reference and suppress the external force. On the other hand, compliance or a force controller should control the external force.

In this paper, we introduce a hybrid ratio, which determines the task of motion. The hybrid ratio HR is defined as follows:

$$
\mathcal {H R} = \frac {\ddot {\theta} _ {m}}{\ddot {\theta} ^ {\mathrm{ext}}}.\tag{11}
$$

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 3. Robust acceleration control system.

TABLE I

HYBRID RATIO AND CONTROL STIFFNESS

|  | Hybrid ratio | Control Stiffness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Force control | 1 | 0 |
| Compliance control | $0 < \mathcal{HR} < 1$ | $0 < \kappa < \infty$ |
| Position control | 0 | ∞ |

The hybrid ratio represents the influence of the external acceleration input on the acceleration response of the system.

The ideal position control should have 0 hybrid ratio; however, the ideal force feedback control should have 1 hybrid ratio. The comparison between the hybrid ratio and the control stiffness is listed, as shown in Table I. From Table I, it turns out that it is easy to set the intermediate value between force control and position control by using the hybrid ratio.

## B. Mode Quarry Matrix

The interaction mode control considers only the interaction between systems. The interactions are abstracted by using the mode quarry matrices [21]–[23]. The mode quarry matrices transform each physical parameter of systems into a modal parameter. The modal decomposition is attained by using the mode quarry matrices as follows:

$$
Q _ {1} = 1\tag{12}
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {Q} _ {2} = \frac {1}{2} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & - 1 \end{array} \right]\tag{13}
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {Q} _ {3} = \frac {1}{3} \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & - 1 \\ 2 & - 1 & - 1 \end{array} \right]\tag{14}
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {Q} _ {4} = \frac {1}{4} \left[ \begin{array}{c c c c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & - 1 \\ 0 & 2 & - 1 & - 1 \\ 3 & - 1 & - 1 & - 1 \end{array} \right]\tag{15}
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {Q} _ {5} = \frac {1}{5} \left[ \begin{array}{c c c c c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & - 1 & - 1 \\ 0 & 3 & - 1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ 4 & - 1 & - 1 & - 1 & - 1 \end{array} \right]\tag{16}
$$

where $Q _ { \mathrm { 1 } } { - } Q _ { \mathrm { 5 } }$ are the mode quarry matrices.

The first row of the mode quarry matrices represents the common mode of all systems. The succeeding rows represent the differential modes of systems. Thus, it is possible to apply the mode quarry matrices to an infinite-dimensional system, which is given by

$$
\boldsymbol {Q} _ {n} = \frac {1}{n} \left[ \begin{array}{c c c c c c c} 1 & 1 & 1 & \dots & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 1 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 2 & - 1 & - 1 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & n - 2 & - 1 & \dots & - 1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ n - 1 & - 1 & - 1 & \dots & - 1 & - 1 & - 1 \end{array} \right].\tag{17}
$$

From (12) to (17), it is easy to extend the order of the mode quarry matrix. The order of the mode quarry matrices corresponds to the task DOF of multirobot systems.

Since the product of the mode quarry matrix and the transpose of the mode quarry matrix yields an orthogonal matrix, the mode quarry matrices have orthogonality. Thus, the abstracted modes are independent of each other. The modal acceleration reference is easily integrated and distributed into each system by using the inverse matrices of the mode quarry matrices.

## C. Controller Design of Multirobot Systems

The controller design of multirobot systems by interaction mode control is shown in Fig. 4. Fig. 4 shows a general structure of the interaction mode control of multirobot systems. In this paper, $\ddot{\theta}_{ij}^{ ref }(i = A \sim N,j = 1 \sim N),\ddot{\theta}_{ij}(i = A \sim N,j =$ $1 \sim N )$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \ddot { \theta } _ { i j } ^ { \mathrm { e x t } } ( i = A \sim N , j = 1 \sim N ) } \end{array}$ denote the acceleration references, the acceleration responses, and the equivalent accelerations of the external force with respect to the joint coordinate system, respectively. The subscript shows the system number and the actuator number of each system. Each actuator is controlled by the robust acceleration control, as shown in Fig. 3. The acceleration responses and the equivalent accelerations of the external force are transformed into work space accelerations $\ddot { \pmb x } _ { i } ( i = A \sim N )$ and $\ddot { \pmb x } _ { i } ^ { \mathrm { e x t } } ( i = A \sim N )$ by using the Jacobian matrices as in (5). The mode quarry matrices abstract the interactions between multirobot systems, and each acceleration of the system is transformed into modal accelerations m¨ and $\dot { m } ^ { \mathrm { e x t } }$

Since the transformed modes are independent to each other, it is possible to design a controller only in the modal space. It is possible to realize the assigned hybrid ratio in each mode according to the task. The motion command with the hybrid ratio is represented as task code. The acceleration references in each mode $\dot { m } ^ { \mathrm { r e f } }$ are integrated and realized in each joint system through the inverse modal transformation.

The proposed interaction mode control is effective for the integration of various control stiffnesses by multirobot systems such as grasping motion [11] and bilateral and/or multilateral teleoperation [29]–[31]. Thus, the interaction mode control is able to be treated as task kinematics.

## IV. CONTROLLER DESIGN OF GRASPING MOTION

## A. Controller Design by Interaction Mode Control

In this section, the proposed interaction mode control is applied for grasping motion by three linear motor systems. The controller design of grasping motion by interaction mode control is shown in Fig. 5. Since each linear motor system has one-DOF motion, transformation from the joint space to the work space is not required.

Each acceleration response and its equivalent acceleration of the external force are transformed into modal space by using the third-order mode quarry matrix $\mathbf { Q } _ { 3 }$ , which is given by

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \ddot {m} _ {1} \\ \ddot {m} _ {2} \\ \ddot {m} _ {3} \end{array} \right] = \frac {1}{3} \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & - 1 \\ 2 & - 1 & - 1 \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} \ddot {x} _ {A} \\ \ddot {x} _ {B} \\ \ddot {x} _ {C} \end{array} \right] \\ \left[ \begin{array}{c} \ddot {m} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ext}} \\ \ddot {m} _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{ext}} \\ \ddot {m} _ {3} ^ {\mathrm{ext}} \end{array} \right] = \frac {1}{3} \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & - 1 \\ 2 & - 1 & - 1 \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} \ddot {x} _ {A} ^ {\mathrm{ext}} \\ \ddot {x} _ {B} ^ {\mathrm{ext}} \\ \ddot {x} _ {C} ^ {\mathrm{ext}} \end{array} \right] \end{array}\tag{18}
$$

(19)

where $\ddot { x } _ { i } ( i = A \sim C )$ denotes the acceleration of each system, $\ddot { m } _ { i } ( i = 1 \sim 3 )$ denotes the accelerations of each mode.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 6. Grasping motion by three robot systems.

The superscript ext denotes the equivalent acceleration of the external force.

The transformed three modes are shown in Fig. 6. The modes of the grasping motion by three robot systems correspond to the center-of-gravity (COG) control mode, the yawing control mode, and the internal control mode, respectively. The hybrid ratio in each mode is assigned as follows:

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c} \mathcal {H R} _ {1} \\ \mathcal {H R} _ {2} \\ \mathcal {H R} _ {3} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \frac {\ddot {m} _ {1}}{\dddot {m} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ext}}} \\ \frac {\ddot {m} _ {2}}{\dddot {m} _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{ext}}} \\ \frac {\dot {m} _ {3}}{\dddot {m} _ {3} ^ {\mathrm{ext}}} \end{array} \right]\tag{20}
$$

$$
\mathcal {H R} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right].\tag{21}
$$

The hybrid ratio $[ 0 \; 0 \; 1 ] ^ { T }$ represents the grasping task code.

It is possible to attain hybrid force/position control or impedance control in one mode by setting the hybrid ratio between 0 and 1. However, the focus of this paper is in the integrated design of hybrid force/position motion with respect to modal space. Each decoupled mode controls pure force or position, and this paper shows that integrated motion is achieved based on acceleration control.

According to the hybrid ratio, the modal controllers $C_{i}(s)(i = 1 \sim 3)$ are designed as follows:

$$
C _ {1} (s) = \frac {1}{s ^ {2}} K _ {p 1} + \frac {1}{s} K _ {v 1}\tag{22}
$$

$$
C _ {2} (s) = \frac {1}{s ^ {2}} K _ {p 2} + \frac {1}{s} K _ {v 2}\tag{23}
$$

$$
C _ {3} (s) = K _ {f 3}\tag{24}
$$

where $K _ { p i } ( i = 1 , 2 )$ denotes the position control gain, and $K _ { v i } ( i = 1 , 2 )$ denotes the velocity control gain, respectively. $K _ { f 3 }$ denotes the force control gain.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

TABLE II

CONTROL PARAMETERS OF SIMULATIONS

| $C_1(s)$ | Mode 1 controller | $=2500\frac{1}{s^2}+100\frac{1}{s}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $C_2(s)$ | Mode 2 controller | $=400\frac{1}{s^2}+40\frac{1}{s}$ |
| $C_3(s)$ | Mode 3 controller | =5.0 |
| $g_{dis}$ | Cut-off frequency of the disturbance observer | 2000 rad/s |
| $g_{pd}$ | Cut-off frequency of the pseudo derivation | 3000 rad/s |

When the hybrid ratio is 1, the system is based on force control. In force control, the gain of the force control is regarded as the inverse of the equivalent mass of the system. To improve force control performance, the force gain should be enlarged. The limitation is determined by observation noise.

On the contrary, when the hybrid ratio is 0, the system is based on position control. It is required to enlarge the control stiffness to improve the position control performance. Since the position controller is based on PD control, the position and velocity control gains should be enlarged as much as possible. Its limitation is determined by torque saturation.

The modal acceleration references by the modal controllers are realized and distributed into three robot systems by using the inverse matrix of the mode quarry matrix.

## B. Simulation

To confirm the validity of the proposed method, the following simulations are conducted.

• Simulation 1:

Case. 1 (0–0.5 s): grasping task + COG step control.

Case. 2 (0.5–1 s): grasping task + COG step control + yawing position control.

Fig. 7. Simulation results of grasping motion (step responses). (a) Position responses. (b) Force responses. (c) Mode 1, 2 responses. (d) Mode 3 response.

• Simulation 2:

Case. 1 (0–0.5 s): grasping task + COG frequency control (2 Hz).

Case. 2 (0.5–1 s): grasping task + COG frequency control (2 Hz) + yawing step control.

The grasping object is cylinder, and the radius is 0.15 m. The stiffness of the object is 100 N/m. The initial positions of each system are −0.1, 0.05, and 0.05 m. The grasping force command of the internal control mode is set to 5 N. The control parameters of the simulation are listed as Table II.

1) Simulation 1: The simulation results of the COG step responses are shown in Fig. 7. The position responses and force responses of each system are shown in Fig. 7(a) and (b), respectively. The modal responses of position and force are shown in Fig. 7(c) and (d), respectively.

From Fig. 7(d), it turns out that the internal force is well controlled to 5 N regardless of the COG position. The COG position and the yawing position are controlled by the position servoing. The response times of the COG control and yawing control are set independently. As a result, the grasping motion is assured by the interaction mode control.

2) Simulation 2: The simulation results of the COG frequency responses are shown in Fig. 8. The COG position command is given as a sinusoidal wave, and the frequency is 2 Hz. The position responses and force responses of each system are shown in Fig. 8(a) and (b), respectively. The modal responses of position and force are shown in Fig. 7(c) and (d), respectively.

From the simulation results, the internal force responses of the frequency responses [Fig. 7(d)] equal the responses of the step responses [Fig. 7(d)], although the command of the other mode is changed. It turns out that the responses of the yawing control mode are also independent from the COG controller.

## C. Experiment

1) Experimental Setup: The proposed interaction mode control is applied for three linear motor systems, which are shown in Fig. 9. The linear motor is rod type, and there is little friction effect. The external force is observed by the disturbance observer without force sensors. Only a linear encoder is implemented as the sensor of the system. The resolution of the position encoder is 0.1 µm. The experimental parameters are listed in Table III. Object information is an unknown parameter in the control system. The control software is written in C language under RT–Linux 3.2. The sampling time is 100 µs.

2) Experimental Results: The following experiments of co-operative transportation by three robot systems are conducted:

• Case. 1 (0–3 s) Moving task;

• Case. 2 (3–6 s) Grasping task;

• Case. 3 (6–8 s) Grasping task + COG frequency control (2 Hz);

• Case. 4 (8–10 s) Grasping task + COG frequency control (5 Hz) + yawing frequency control (2 Hz).

In Case. 1, since the moving task is assigned in the robot systems, the task code is set to $[ 0 \; 0 \; 0 ] ^ { T }$ . Thus, position control is designed in all modes. From Fig. 10(c), the robot systems are moved according to the shape of the object. The position responses of the internal control mode is well regulated to −0.005 m.

In Case. 2, the task code is changed from the moving task to the grasping task. The task code of the grasping task is $[ 0   0   1 ] ^ { T }$ The switching motion from position control to force control is easily achieved by changing the hybrid ratio, since the control system is based on acceleration control. The force command of the grasping force is 1 N. From Fig. 10(d), suddenly varying force is observed in force response; however, it is only the impact force at the collision with the object. Since the control stiffness in internal mode is 0, the effect may not lose stability. As a result, it turns out that the internal force is well controlled to 1 N.

| $K_{fn}$ | Force constant | 3.3 N/A |
| $C_1(s)$ | Mode 1 controller | =2500$\frac{1}{s^2}$+100$\frac{1}{s}$ |
| $C_2(s)$ | Mode 2 controller | =400$\frac{1}{s^2}$+40$\frac{1}{s}$ |
| $C_3(s)$ | Mode 3 controller (Case. 1) | =2500$\frac{1}{s^2}$+100$\frac{1}{s}$ |
| $C_3(s)$ | Mode 3 controller (Case. 2 ~ 4) | =1.0 |
| $g_{dis}$ | Cut-off frequency of disturbance observer | 2000 rad/s |
| $g_{pd}$ | Cut-off frequency of pseudo derivation | 3000 rad/s |

In Case. 3, the COG position command is given as a sinusoidal wave. The command frequency and vibrational amplitude in the COG control mode are 2 Hz and 0.004 m, respectively. From Fig. 10(c), the COG position is changed according to the command in the COG control mode. From Fig. 10(d), it turns out that the internal force is controlled regardless of the changes of the COG position. In the internal mode, the reaction force from the object is controlled to grasp it. On the contrary, in the COG and yawing modes, this effect acts as unknown disturbance and is suppressed. As a result, the validity of the adaptive motion in an unknown environment is confirmed.

Finally, in Case. 4, the COG position command is changed to 5 Hz, and the yawing position are controlled by the position servoing. The command frequency and vibrational amplitude in the yawing control mode are 2 Hz and 0.006 m, respectively. From Fig. 10(c), it is possible to attain the desired motions of the COG control mode and yawing control mode, independently. The grasping task is assured, since the grasping force is kept constant.

As a result, the hybrid ratio in each mode is independently realized by interaction mode control. The interaction mode control designs the motion controller of multirobot systems intuitively.

## V. CONCLUSION

This paper has proposed a unified control approach for multirobot systems by interaction mode control. The proposed interaction mode control controls only the interactions between the systems. The interactions are abstracted by using the mode quarry matrices. Since the mode quarry matrices divide systems into decoupled modes, it is possible to design controller in the modal space.

This paper also proposed a novel control index named “hybrid ratio.” Hybrid ratio is defined as the influence of the external acceleration input on the acceleration response of the system. It is possible to realize the assigned hybrid ratio in each mode according to task motions. Thus, the motion command with the hybrid ratio is represented as task code.

The proposed interaction mode control was applied for grasping motion by multirobot systems. The numerical and experimental results showed the viability of the proposed method.

**Seiichiro Katsura** (S’03–M’04) received the B.E. degree in system design engineering and the M.E. and Ph.D. degrees in integrated design engineering from Keio University, Yokohama, Japan, in 2001, 2002, and 2004, respectively.

From 2003 to 2005, he was a Research Fellow of the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science. From 2004 to 2005, he was a Postdoctoral Fellow with Keio University. Since 2005, he has been with Nagaoka University of Technology, Nagaoka, Japan. His research interests include haptics, motion control, and robotics.

Dr. Katsura received the Best Paper Award from the Institute of Electrical Engineers of Japan (IEEJ) in 2003 and the Dr. Yasujiro Niwa Outstanding Paper Award in 2004. He is a member of the IEEJ, Society of Instrument and Control Engineers, Japan Society of Mechanical Engineers, and Robotics Society of Japan.

**Kiyoshi Ohishi** (M’86) received the B.E., M.E., and Ph.D. degrees in electrical engineering from Keio University, Yokohama, Japan, in 1981, 1983, and 1986, respectively.

From 1986 to 1993, he was an Associate Professor with Osaka Institute of Technology, Osaka, Japan. Since 1993, he has been with Nagaoka University of Technology, Nagaoka, Japan, where he became a Professor in 2003. His research interests include power electronics, mechatronics, and motion control.

Dr. Ohishi received the Outstanding Paper Award at IECON’85 and Best Paper Awards at IECON’02 and IECON’04 from the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society. He also received the Best Paper Award from the Institute of Electrical Engineers of Japan (IEEJ) in 2002. He is a Senior Member of the IEEJ and is a member of the Society of Instrument and Control Engineers, Japan Society of Mechanical Engineers, and Robotics Society of Japan.
